shots.vo: First, white light isn't really white. It's every colour, mixed together.

shots.vo: Each colour is a wave. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue and violet have short, tight ones.

shots.vo: Eighteen fifty-nine. An Irish scientist, John Tyndall, shines a beam of light through a glass tube of fine mist in his lab.

shots.vo: Years later, Lord Rayleigh, an English physicist, works out the maths. Tiny particles, smaller than the light's waves, scatter short waves far more than long ones.

shots.negative: letters, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Blue light gets scattered almost six times more than red. Violet, even more.
Our air is full of tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules. As sunlight passes through, they knock the blue light in every direction.
shots.prompt: sunlight streaming down through the atmosphere seen from a high mountain top, the sky glowing blue all around, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: So wherever you look, blue light is coming at you from all over the sky. That's the blue you see.

shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: But wait. If violet scatters even more, why isn't the sky violet?

shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: The sun gives out less violet than blue. Some of it is absorbed high up in the atmosphere. And your eyes are much more sensitive to blue.

shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Now, the sunset. Here's the twist. It's the same effect.

shots.vo: At noon, sunlight crosses a thin slice of air. At sunset it comes in sideways, through far more atmosphere. By the time it reaches you, the blue has been scattered away.
What's left is the light that survives the long trip. Orange. Red.

shots.vo: Dust and smoke make it stronger. That's why sunsets after wildfires or volcanic eruptions can look unreal.

shots.vo: And on Mars, fine dust in the thin air turns it around. A butterscotch sky by day. A blue sunset.
NASA's Curiosity rover has photographed it. A cold blue glow around a setting sun, on another world.

shots.vo: So the next time someone tells you the sky reflects the ocean, you'll know. It's sunlight bouncing off the air itself.
